unit.title: Volume, surface area and symmetry
unit.blurb: Volume of prisms and cylinders, surface area of triangular prisms, pyramids and cylinders, and planes of symmetry in 3D shapes.
unit.subject: maths

O1.t: Use V = area of cross-section × length to find the volume of prisms and cylinders, and solve problems.

O2.t: Find the surface area of triangular prisms, pyramids and cylinders, using nets.

O3.t: Identify planes of symmetry in 3D shapes.

lesson.t: How do I find the volume of a prism?
p: **Volume = area of cross-section × length.** It works for any prism because the cross-section is the same all the way through.
The triangular prism shown has a triangle with base 8 cm and height 5 cm and length 12 cm: (½ × 8 × 5) × 12 = 20 × 12 = 240 cm³.
A **cylinder** is a prism with a circular cross-section: **V = πr²h**.

lesson.t: How do I solve volume problems?
p: Step 1: Identify the cross-section and find its area.
Step 2: Multiply by the length (or height).
Step 3: Convert units if needed: 1000 cm³ = 1 litre.
Step 4: For missing lengths, rearrange: length = volume ÷ cross-section area.

lesson.t: What is the surface area of a cylinder?
p: Unroll the curved surface: it becomes a **rectangle** of width 2πr (the circumference) and height h.
**Curved surface area = 2πrh.** **Total surface area = 2πr² + 2πrh** (two circles + the curved part).

lesson.t: What is a plane of symmetry?
p: A **plane of symmetry** cuts a 3D shape into two halves that are **mirror images** of each other.
The cuboid shown (all edges different) has **3** planes of symmetry: one parallel to each pair of faces.

lesson.t: How many planes do common solids have?
How do I find the planes of symmetry?
p: Step 1: Imagine slicing the solid with a flat sheet so the two halves are mirror images.
Step 2: Try planes parallel to faces and through opposite edges or diagonals.
Step 3: Count only the planes that work.

lesson.q: Explain why a cube has 9 planes of symmetry.

p: A plane is a flat slice through the whole solid, not a line on one face.
Imagine cutting the shape with a knife – if the pieces match like mirror images, it is a plane of symmetry.
